content.title: Dylan Betts Carrying on his Sisters’ USA Basketball Legacies is a Tall Order - USA Basketball
content.text: Skip to main contentDylan Betts was in his last class at Cherry Creek High School in Greenwood Village, Colorado, when his mother, Michelle, informed him that he’d been invited to USA Basketball’s 2025 Men’s Junior National Team April minicamp in San Antonio, Texas. “It means a lot to me,” Betts said of being one of 65 athletes invited to the minicamp. “Definitely, it’s very hard to be selected. Lots of good competition out here. You’ve got to be confident and [not] be scared of anybody.” At just 15 years old, Betts turns heads before he even laces up his sneakers. Standing at a staggering 7-foot-2, it may not be hard for him to reach the heights that his sisters, Lauren and Sienna, reached in their times with USA Basketball. Lauren, Betts’ eldest sibling and the force behind UCLA’s 2025 NCAA Women’s Final Four run, has played for three USA women’s national teams since beginning her journey with USA Basketball in 2018. The 6-foot-7 college junior won two FIBA gold medals in 2021 and 2019, and a silver medal in 2023. Sienna, a standout in the Class of 2025 and a future Bruin, won a gold medal at the 2024 FIBA U18 Women’s AmeriCup and was more recently announced as a member of the 2025 USA Nike Hoop Summit Team, which competes next weekend in Portland, Oregon. “You definitely learn a lot as you watch them,” Betts said of his sisters. “They’re very talented and they obviously know a lot. Watching both of them, you just learn what it takes to be a USA Basketball player and the communication you need, everything. All the confidence, and [they] just give off details on how to be a good USA Basketball player. It’s a good role model.” It isn’t just his sisters’ USA Basketball torch that he’s carrying. Betts hails from a family of distinguished athletes. His father, Andrew, was a 7-foot-1 standout at Long Beach State and was taken in the second round of the 1998 NBA Draft before enjoying a 14-year professional career overseas. His mom was a volleyball star at Long Beach, where she met Andrew, and won a national championship with the 49ers in 1998 as part of an undefeated season. Athleticism runs in the family. So, it’s no coincidence that Betts is set up for success at such a young age. He’s already the tallest in the family, and yet, much like his ceiling as a basketball player, Betts still feels like he has room to grow – remarkably so. “I think maybe a few more inches – like one or two more,” Betts said. “My growth plates are still open [is what] I’ve heard, so maybe a few more inches.” It’s easy to imagine that a prospect of Betts’ stature is no stranger to comparison. His astounding height, daunting length, defensive identity and uncanny ability to be light on his feet, though, is a skill set unique to one particular anomaly – San Antonio Spurs phenom Victor Wembanyama. “A lot of people at my school call me ‘Wemby,’” Betts noted, chuckling at the thought. “On my Instagram they call me ‘Wemby disciple’ or something like that. Definitely a lot of comparisons.” But Betts is striving to create his own path and it started in April’s minicamp. With his parents laying the foundation and sisters setting the benchmark for success, Betts is ready for all that comes with USA Basketball. “I’m looking forward to hopefully being with USA (Basketball) more and more and hopefully winning a gold medal, getting camp invites, (being selected for the) Hoop Summit, all of that. “I just want to accomplish everything that goes into USA Basketball.” Related Articles
